newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany's Hoechst still under fire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany's Hoechst still under fire.

text.p: German Hoechst AG continued to draw investor ire on Thursday, one day after the chemicals and drugs giant disappointed the market with weaker earnings and news it had shelved plans to float its HMR drugs unit.

Hoechst shares dipped two percent to close bourse trade down at 68.80 marks as traders were still angry, saying Europe's largest chemicals misled them on last year's earnings and had backtracked on a promise to bring their biggest prize, the drugs unit, to market.
But analysts, not mincing words about the company's poor disclosure policy, also stressed Hoechst's fundamental strategy remained solid, signalling the share market bloodletting should end soon.
"Strategically Hoechst did the correct thing, but after having said something so blatant, their U-turn looks weak," said Peter Blair, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.

Hoechst shares, outperforming the German industry sector by 1.8 percent over the last 12 months until Monday, had been largely propelled by analysts' delight that the formerly staid, chemical giant was finally tackling an overdue restructuring.

Spurred by Hoechst officials' unbroken optimism and insistence the massive overhaul, involving the integration of newly acquired groups and spin-offs of other businesses, was proceeding faster than expected, market expectations had reached unrealistic highs, analysts admitted.
Nonetheless they faulted Hoechst for not taking quick action when it became clear that 400 million marks ($236 million) of restructuring costs in the fourth quarter would lead to a loss.
Hoechst posted a 383 million mark fourth quarter loss and a lower-than-expected 1996 operating profit of 4.013 billion marks and a two percent drop in sales to 50.9 billion marks.

"A profit-warning, some hints in an interview that there was trouble with the numbers, or even a more detailed breakdown of the extraordinary gains and losses when the core numbers were released would have helped," said another analyst.
After meeting Hoechst executives on Wednesday, several analysts were disgruntled with what they called they company's cavalier reporting policies.
"If they want to list their shares in New York, these sorts of procedures cannot go on," another analyst complained.

Analysts also worried Hoechst would continue to backpedal on other ambitious goals, like reaching target margins of 20 percent by 1998 in the drugs division as Hoechst plans to clean out the generics business and pay for the Roussel integration.
"Hoechst promised more than it delivered, they have let people down on earnings and the dividend payment, and it will take a long time to rebuild confidence," said Salomon's Blair.

However, analysts gave Hoechst high marks for stopping short of being forced to make a wrong decision by floating the drugs unit prematurely and said investors will realise this, allowing the share price to stabilise.

"Fundamentally there is no reason for the Hoechst share price to drop below 65 marks," said Thomas Schiessle, analyst at Delbrueck & Co in Frankfurt, explaining that investors' momentary anger should make way for more rational decisions.
"The questions have to be, is the strategy still on track and can management implement the strategy? And the answer to both questions is yes," Schiessle added.
Some analysts even suggested that the issue of a public listing for the drugs unit HMR may be revisited in the future, once the unit is further along in reaching its goals.

"If they listed HMR now, it could be dangerous as the price earnings ratio would be low, leaving HMR cheap and vulnerable to a hostile takeover," Delbrueck's Schiessle said, stressing top managers did not rule out the option altogether.
"Everyone has to realise that the clean-up task at Hoechst is going to take more time and that results cannot possibly occur as quickly as a euphoric market had hoped."
($ = 1.695 German Marks)
